<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line" lang="en">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"> Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tencent Hy Visual Generation Team
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. We present<span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> Hy-Nomas</span>, a video world model with an 8B diffusion backbone that supports free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns. It generates variable-length segments conditioned on current inputs and cached history. Our central design aligns structured video captions with action-aware causal attention: descriptive context remains accessible across segments, while action instructions are restricted to their intended temporal windows. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer (PE) translates user requests and multimodal interaction histories into structured conditions for the next segment. A multi-stage curriculum progressively introduces causal generation, text interaction, camera control, and training on model-generated histories, followed by diffusion distillation. In human evaluation,  Hy-Nomas shows superior performance over existing world models. We release model weights, code and benchmarks, together with a lightweight adaptation workflow, to support reproducible research on interactive world generation.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<blockquote id="p1.1" class="ltx_quote"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:6.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span>
</blockquote>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent ltx_align_center">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p2.1.1" class="ltx_text"><a href="https://hy-nomas.hy.tencent.com/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href"><span class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-1.5pt;"><img src="2610.36729v1/logo/hunyuan-logo.png" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:15/15;" width="15" height="15" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></span> Project Page</a>  <span id="p2.1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">|</span>  <a href="https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-Nomas" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href"><span class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-1.5pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.36729v1/hf-logo.svg" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:16/15;" width="16" height="15"></object></span> Model Weights</a>
  <span id="p2.1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">|</span>  <a href="https://huggingface.co/datasets/tencent/Hy-Nomas-Bench" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href"><span class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-1.5pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.36729v1/hf-logo.svg" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:16/15;" width="16" height="15"></object></span> Benchmarks</a>  <span id="p2.1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">|</span>  <a href="https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-Nomas" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href"><span class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-1.5pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.36729v1/github-logo.svg" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:15/15;" width="15" height="15"></object></span> Code</a></span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.36729v1/teaser.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/302;" width="476" height="302" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Interactive world generation with  Hy-Nomas.</span> Free-form text instructions and continuous camera control can be interleaved across successive interaction turns. At each turn, a vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts the user request and observed world history into a structured text prompt and a duration for the next video segment. Conditioned on these inputs and cached context,  Hy-Nomas autoregressively generates the next segment, allowing the world to unfold through continued interaction.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contents</span></p>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We define a video world model as an interactive virtual environment that renders visual observations of future states in response to user commands. Users observe the current world, decide how to act, and the model generates new visual observations that reflect both their commands and the preceding interaction history. This closed interaction loop extends the objective of conventional video generation, where a fixed prompt typically specifies a short video clip in advance. An interactive world must accommodate input commands that arrive during generation, model action-dependent dynamics, and preserve the consequences of earlier actions.
Recent systems, including Genie 3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google DeepMind, 2025</a>)</cite>, HappyOyster <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alibaba Cloud, 2026</a>)</cite> and LingBot-World v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>, have made substantial progress in navigation, semantic intervention, and long-horizon generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib101" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bolton et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib102" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bar et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Building on these advances, we introduce  Hy-Nomas, an 8B-parameter world model focused on execution of free-form text instructions and their integration with camera navigation across multi-turn interactions.  Hy-Nomas enables users to direct both what happens in a world and how they explore it through one generative backbone.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Building such a model requires more than simply replacing full attention with a causal mask. A pretrained bidirectional diffusion transformer (DiT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2023</a>)</cite> must be adapted to generate successive segments from available history while following the current user command, preventing information leakage that breaks causality, and supporting efficient reuse of cached context <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin and others, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu and others, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao and others, 2026</a>)</cite>. Because each generated segment becomes evidence for the next, small errors can compound into appearance drift, implausible motion, and scene breakdown; training must therefore prepare the model for its own imperfect predictions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang and others, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib104" title="" class="ltx_ref">Decart et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Multi-turn interaction adds a second difficulty: persistent scene information must remain accessible, while an action instruction should take effect only during its intended time interval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen and others, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib106" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mao et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang and others, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib128" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The model must also coordinate free-form semantic commands with geometric camera controls, and retain identities, layouts, and state changes when previously observed content returns into view <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. Finally, temporally causal information flow alone does not establish physical causality. Learning plausible action-to-state transitions requires training data that connects actions with their observable consequences and evaluation that tests these behaviors across successive interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib103" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ying et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib109" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2026a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib108" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Hy-Nomas can generate visual worlds with different styles and viewpoints, supporting minute-scale rollouts with successive instructions for subject actions, object interactions, scene changes and camera motion, as shown in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Free-form text prompts and camera control commands can be interleaved within the same session, with historical visual and semantic context carried forward through the autoregressive key-value (KV) cache. A vision-language model (VLM), the Prompt Enhancer (PE) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib110" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026b</a>)</cite> converts the user’s request and current observations into a structured prompt with an appropriate duration for the next segment. Our evaluation demonstrates that  Hy-Nomas is superior to existing world models across a range of interactive tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We build  Hy-Nomas by co-designing our data strategy, video captioning, model architecture, and training strategy towards free-form interactive world generation. Our data pipeline sources videos with physical interaction, human and object motion, camera movement, and long-range dependencies; video captioning records persistent subject identities, scene changes, and timestamped actions, complemented by estimated camera trajectories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. The model architecture design couples these annotations with action-aware causal attention. Descriptive text remains available across subsequent segments, while action-specific text is restricted to its originating segment and annotated time window. This separation is designed to retain descriptive context and the visual consequences of an action without repeatedly reissuing the action itself. Mixed text-only and camera-conditioned training supports transitions between two interaction modes. Starting from HunyuanVideo 1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we progressively introduce segment causality, localized action conditioning, and camera control, followed by high-quality annealing and segment forcing into the model training process. To make this training practical, we combine a high-compression video autoencoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, FLOPs-balanced packing of variable-length videos <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krell et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, attention kernels that execute heterogeneous masks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib92" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tao and Huang, 2025</a>)</cite>, distributed sequence and model-state sharding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jacobs et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">PyTorch Contributors, </a>)</cite>, and stage-dependent memory management, supporting packed sequences of up to <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="360K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>360</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">360K</annotation></semantics></math> tokens. Bounded-cache inference and a LoRA workflow that transfers adapters from the base model to its distilled counterpart further support deployment and customization for downstream applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our main contributions are:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:15pt;">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">An interactive 8B world model.</span> We develop  Hy-Nomas for multi-turn free-form interaction and continuous camera navigation within one autoregressive DiT.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Aligned supervision and action conditioning.</span> We combine structured chronological captions, persistent subject descriptions, timestamped actions,
and camera trajectories with action-aware causal attention that distinguishes enduring context from temporally localized
instructions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A scalable training recipe and open-weight model.</span> We integrate a progressive strategy to gradually extend the model’s capability, together with bounded-cache inference and lightweight downstream adaptation. We release model weights and code to support further research.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation of world-model capabilities.</span> We assess multi-turn text interaction, camera navigation, interleaved control, and spatial memory, demonstrating the advantages of  Hy-Nomas while identifying the remaining challenges in world modeling. We release all the benchmarks to facilitate reproducible research on world-model evaluation.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Data</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct a large-scale, heterogeneous video corpus spanning real and virtual environments. Our end-to-end pipeline converts raw videos into training samples through standardized preprocessing, filtering, semantic deduplication, camera-trajectory annotation, and structured captioning. We adjust the sampling distribution across training stages to address weaknesses identified in each stage. Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 Data ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes the pipeline.</p>
</div>

5</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#667583;--ltx-fill-color:#667583;" fill="#667583" stroke="#667583" transform="matrix(1.4 0.0 0.0 1.4 1032.2 5</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Data pipeline.</span> Raw videos are split, transcoded, and filtered by basic video properties and visual quality. Hierarchical clustering supports within-cluster deduplication, and a VLM assigns labels to each video from a predefined taxonomy. Video tagging adds captions and, for selected clips, camera-trajectory annotations. Across each training stage, adaptive sampling adjusts the training distribution in response to weaknesses identified from evaluations of earlier stages.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Data Filtering</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The raw videos vary in encoding types, duration, frame rate, resolution, and encoding quality. We standardize preprocessing by first dividing each video into 5-minute segments and then splitting these segments at detected shot boundaries. Our shot boundary detector is based on OmniShotCut <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026a</a>)</cite> and fine-tuned on high-quality annotations to improve accuracy in challenging cases. We transcode the resulting clips into a unified format and filter them by basic video properties (e.g., duration, aspect ratio, and resolution) and visual quality metrics (e.g., motion, clarity, and aesthetic scores). Additional filters screen for derivative content and abrupt transitions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Data Distribution</h3>

<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Clustering and deduplication</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We extract a visual embedding for each video using Qwen3-VL-Embedding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, group videos by visual similarity through hierarchical clustering, and apply SemDeDup <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abbas et al., 2023</a>)</cite> within each cluster to remove semantically redundant clips.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Taxonomy labeling</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct a hierarchical taxonomy covering semantic content and visual attributes. Content categories include different types of interaction, object manipulation, human and object movement, and camera motion; visual attributes describe camera perspective, subject type, subject and camera motion patterns, and recording methods. We fine tune a VLM to label each video according to this taxonomy, enabling targeted data selection and sampling along complementary semantic and visual dimensions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Adaptive sampling</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adapt the sampling distribution across training stages to address weaknesses identified in earlier stages. To select relevant data, we associate each video with two sets of labels: predicted video-level taxonomy labels and labels derived from hierarchical clustering. Since visual clustering is unsupervised, we manually annotate clusters at an intermediate level of the hierarchy to make them usable for data selection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Depending on the target content category or visual attribute, we select videos using taxonomy labels, cluster-level annotations, or a combination of both. We then adjust the sampling weights of the selected subsets in subsequent training stages to prioritize areas that need further improvement.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Camera Trajectories</h3>

<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Trajectory annotation</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use ViPE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> to estimate camera trajectories. To manage its substantial computational cost, we apply it to a subset of videos suitable for trajectory estimation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To scale annotation, we upgrade the camera calibration and segmentation modules with more capable pretrained models while retaining the existing depth estimator. We modularize the pipeline and apply adaptive spatiotemporal downsampling to reduce memory usage and improve throughput. We also tune the backend SLAM sliding window and optimization schedules to balance optimization scope against accumulated trajectory drift.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We additionally train a video-based inverse dynamics model (IDM), initialized from a pretrained VPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib100" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baker et al., 2022</a>)</cite> backbone, to predict discrete camera motion (such as WASD keyboard inputs) directly from video. Training combines synthetic camera-motion videos, and ViPE-derived motion labels refined using dense optical flow. Manually annotated shake and zoom data provide additional supervision, and unavailable labels are masked during training. The IDM predictions support camera motion categorization and data filtering, helping identify clips with inconsistent motion labels or unreliable trajectory annotations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Trajectory filtering</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We filter in-the-wild videos both before ViPE estimation to reduce computational cost and afterward to exclude clips with static cameras, shot cuts, lens distortion, or local estimation instabilities. This filtering proceeds in four sequential steps, with only clips that pass each step advancing to the next:</p>
<ol id="S2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:15pt;">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We restrict the optical-flow motion-score range to reject static scenes and abrupt spikes.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the remaining clips, we run CoTracker3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karaev et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to track a uniform grid of points and filter out videos in which the inter-frame displacement of visible points exceeds <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max(H,W)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max(H,W)</annotation></semantics></math> or the median total displacement of tracked points is below <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max(H,W)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max(H,W)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We then use AnyCalib <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tirado-Garín and Civera, 2025</a>)</cite> to jointly estimate per-frame focal length and radial distortion, penalizing clips with excessive focal-length variation, abrupt focal-length changes, overly large focal lengths, or strong distortion.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, retained clips undergo ViPE estimation, followed by a trajectory audit to detect optimization failures and degenerate motion scales. We reject trajectories exhibiting repeated large orientation jumps within local windows, excessive inter-frame viewing-angle offsets, translation
spikes relative to the local mean inter-frame displacement, or insufficient overall camera displacement.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Video Captioning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design structured video captions to preserve subject identity, scene context, and action chronology, with camera motion explicitly tagged for flexible supervision. Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.4 Video Captioning ‣ 2 Data ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Multi-turn annotation ‣ 2.4 Video Captioning ‣ 2 Data ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> illustrates the caption design and multi-turn annotation procedure.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S2.F3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structured video captioning.</span> The VLM annotates segments sequentially, maintains subject identities, interleaves scene and camera descriptions chronologically, and records subject actions separately with timestamps. A final text-only turn reviews, translates, and validates the annotations to produce aligned English and Chinese captions. During training, camera-motion sentences and their tags are removed when camera trajectories are available and retained otherwise.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Structured caption</h5>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our captions use structured JSON with video-level and segment-level information. Video-level fields specify visual style, camera perspective, and a shared subject list. Each subject has an explicit identifier and a static profile anchored to its earliest clearly identifiable appearance; subsequent actions and state changes reference this identifier to maintain continuity across segments. Within each segment, scene descriptions and camera-motion sentences are interleaved chronologically in the description field. Subject actions and their visible outcomes are recorded separately, with start and end timestamps for each action.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The first segment establishes the scene; subsequent segments describe changes relative to the preceding segment without repeating unchanged context. Action and camera-motion descriptions are limited to each segment’s temporal boundaries, and action entries form a chronological, non-overlapping sequence. This representation records scene changes and action timing to support segment-wise autoregressive rollout training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Camera-motion description</h5>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We enclose camera-motion sentences in explicit &lt;CameraN&gt; and &lt;/CameraN&gt; tags so they can be selected independently of scene and action descriptions. For training segments with ViPE-estimated trajectories, we remove the camera-motion descriptions and their enclosing tags, using the estimated trajectories for explicit camera-motion supervision. For segments without trajectory annotations, we retain the tagged sentences as textual supervision. This complementary strategy supports camera control through either keyboard inputs mapped to trajectories or natural-language motion instructions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multi-turn annotation</h5>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We generate captions in two stages. First, we extract visual features using V-JEPA 2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Assran et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and divide each clip into shorter segments based on temporal changes in these features. In the second stage, a VLM annotates the segments sequentially in a multi-turn conversation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The first turn establishes the initial scene and subject profiles; subsequent turns describe scene changes and current actions while refining subject identities and video-level labels using accumulated evidence. Previous segments and annotations remain in the conversation context to support temporal and semantic consistency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For subsequent segments, the VLM uses visual evidence only from the current and preceding segments to ground its descriptions and reduce hallucination. After all segments have been processed, a final text-only turn reviews the accumulated annotations, corrects earlier drafts, and resolves inconsistencies while preserving the supplied segment boundaries. It produces the final English caption and a structurally aligned Chinese translation, both following the format in Figure <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Multi-turn annotation ‣ 2.4 Video Captioning ‣ 2 Data ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. In this same turn, the VLM checks the JSON structure, required fields, subject references, tags, segment and action timestamps, and consistency between different language versions, then corrects detected inconsistencies before finalizing the output.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F4" class="ltx_figure">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S2.F4.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structured caption format</span>. Video-level fields define perspective, style, and shared subject profiles. Segment descriptions interleave scene information and camera-tagged motion chronologically, excluding main-subject references. The first segment provides a full description; later segments describe changes. Subject actions and their visible outcomes are recorded separately in action-tagged entries using subject tokens. Action intervals are non-overlapping and remain within segment boundaries.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Caption models</h5>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use different captioning models across training stages to balance annotation cost and caption quality. For data-intensive stages, we employ Gemma 4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemma Team, 2026</a>)</cite> and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026a</a>)</cite> for efficient large-scale captioning. For the annealing stage, where annotation quality is prioritized over throughput, we use Kimi K3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moonshot AI, 2026</a>)</cite> to generate detailed segment-wise annotations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Model Architecture</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hy-Nomas builds upon HunyuanVideo 1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. We introduce segment-wise causal attention for autoregressive world generation (Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Segment-wise Causal Attention ‣ 3 Model Architecture ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>) and camera cross-attention for explicit camera control (Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Camera-Trajectory Conditioning ‣ 3 Model Architecture ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).  Hy-Nomas uses a DCAE-V video autoencoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite><span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          We thank the NVIDIA DC-AE team for generously sharing their model checkpoints and providing valuable support in integrating DC-AE-V into HunyuanVideo 1.5.</span></span></span> and a frozen Qwen2.5-VL-7B text encoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025</a>)</cite> inherited from HunyuanVideo 1.5, followed by a timestep-aware token refiner. Starting from Gaussian noise, the model denoises video latents one segment at a time, conditioned on the current text prompt, an optional camera trajectory, and cached keys and values from preceding segments. A dedicated cross-attention module in each MMDiT block <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Esser et al., 2024</a>)</cite> injects camera conditioning, using video features as queries and frame-aligned camera tokens as keys and values. Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3 Model Architecture ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> illustrates the architecture, and Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Model Architecture ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes its primary configuration.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.36729v1/method_framework_h.svg" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/196;" width="476" height="196"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="S3.F5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Overview of the model architecture.</span>
A structured multi-segment prompt, a video clip, and a camera trajectory are encoded into text, video, and camera tokens, respectively.
Text and video tokens are processed by <math id="S3.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=54" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>54</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=54</annotation></semantics></math> dual-stream MMDiT blocks.
Within each block, segment-wise causal attention with 3D RoPE allows tokens to attend to the current and preceding segments, while diffusion timestep embeddings modulate both streams.
The two streams pass through separate MLPs, and camera cross-attention further conditions the video stream on camera tokens.
During autoregressive generation, keys and values associated with both text and video tokens are stored in the KV cache as context for subsequent segments.
The 3D VAE decoder maps denoised video latents to RGB frames.
Purple, blue, and green denote the text, video, and camera streams, respectively.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S3.T1.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.T1.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">Component</td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">Configuration</td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T1.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">Video autoencoder</td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">DCAE-V, <math id="S3.T1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="32\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32\times</annotation></semantics></math> spatial and <math id="S3.T1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times</annotation></semantics></math> temporal compression</td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T1.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">Latent representation</td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">32 channels; patch size <math id="S3.T1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 1\times 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 1\times 1</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>

<td id="S3.T1.2.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">2,048 / 8,192</td></tr>

<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Latent video representation</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We encode an RGB video <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 3\times F\times H\times W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 3\times F\times H\times W}</annotation></semantics></math> into a compact spatiotemporal representation using a causal DCAE-V encoder <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z=\mathcal{E}(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 32\times F_{z}\times H_{z}\times W_{z}},\qquad F_{z}=\left\lfloor\frac{F-1}{4}\right\rfloor+1,H_{z}=\left\lfloor\frac{H}{32}\right\rfloor,W_{z}=\left\lfloor\frac{W}{32}\right\rfloor" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>⌊</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>⌋</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>⌊</mo><mfrac><mi>H</mi><mn>32</mn></mfrac><mo>⌋</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>⌊</mo><mfrac><mi>W</mi><mn>32</mn></mfrac><mo>⌋</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z=\mathcal{E}(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 32\times F_{z}\times H_{z}\times W_{z}},\qquad F_{z}=\left\lfloor\frac{F-1}{4}\right\rfloor+1,H_{z}=\left\lfloor\frac{H}{32}\right\rfloor,W_{z}=\left\lfloor\frac{W}{32}\right\rfloor</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">with spatial and temporal compression factors of <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. Here, <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of frames, while <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> denote the height and width of each frame, respectively. Each latent position is treated as an individual token (<math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 1\times 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 1\times 1</annotation></semantics></math> patch) and linearly projected to the DiT hidden dimension of <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2048" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2048</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2048</annotation></semantics></math>. The diffusion transformer operates directly in this latent space, with the resulting denoised representation decoded back into RGB video by a decoder <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Structured text conditioning</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During preprocessing, each video segment is annotated with a structured JSON caption, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.4 Video Captioning ‣ 2 Data ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. A frozen Qwen2.5-VL-7B encoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025</a>)</cite> extracts segment-wise text embeddings, which are subsequently processed by a two-layer, timestep-conditioned token refiner. Specifically, the embeddings are projected from 3,584 to the MMDiT hidden dimension of 2,048, followed by adaptive modulation conditioned on the diffusion timestep and pooled text context. The resulting refined embeddings serve as text tokens for attention in the MMDiT backbone.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
