(a) Tokens attend to all video and text tokens in the current
and preceding segments.
(b) Action-aware masking further restricts access to action-specific
text tokens.
Colors indicate query-to-key modality pairs; gray cells are masked.
<span id="S3.F6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">head</span> denotes the environment description for the current segment,
and <math id="S3.F6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{0},\ldots,a_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{0},\ldots,a_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> denote actions within that segment.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Flow-matching objective</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The model is trained with linear flow matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Given a clean video latent <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math>, Gaussian noise <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{t}=(1-t)Z+t\epsilon,\qquad V_{t}=\epsilon-Z." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{t}=(1-t)Z+t\epsilon,\qquad V_{t}=\epsilon-Z.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The network predicts the velocity <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> along this path. At inference time, the reverse ODE is initialized from Gaussian noise at <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1</annotation></semantics></math> and integrated toward <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0</annotation></semantics></math> using 100 Euler steps. Classifier-free text guidance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho and Salimans, 2022</a>)</cite> and camera guidance are applied during integration. The resulting clean 32-channel latent is finally decoded by <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain the RGB video.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Segment-wise Causal Attention</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike conventional video generation, video-based world models simulate evolving world states in temporal order, requiring a causal modeling framework. However, the fully bidirectional attention in our base text-to-video (T2V) model does not enforce this causal structure. We therefore replace it with segment-wise causal attention aligned with the temporal structure of the input captions. Specifically, each caption includes explicit temporal boundaries that partition the video and text tokens into temporally aligned semantic segments. Attention is bidirectional within each segment and causal across segments, allowing tokens to attend only to the current and preceding segments. We illustrate this design in Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Structured text conditioning ‣ 3 Model Architecture ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>(a). Query tokens in segment <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> can attend to all key and value tokens from the current and preceding segments <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0,\ldots,j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0,\ldots,j</annotation></semantics></math>, but not to future segments, enforcing causal information flow when modeling evolving world states.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We adapt the bidirectional attention to segment-wise causal attention during the early training stages. However, we observe two limitations of this masking design:</p>
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:15pt;">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Within-segment action misalignment.</span> We observe that actions within a segment can occur in the wrong temporal order. This behavior stems from unrestricted attention to text tokens within each segment: query tokens can attend to the entire segment caption, including actions happening from a different time. This weakens the temporal alignment between video tokens and their corresponding action descriptions in the same segment.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cross-segment action repetition.</span> We also observe that previously generated actions can recur across segments as generation progresses. This behavior is rooted in the continued accessibility of past action descriptions: video tokens in later segments can still attend to action descriptions from earlier segments, prompting the model to replay past actions.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To address these issues, we introduce <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">action-aware causal attention</span>, which extends segment-wise causal attention with a finer-grained masking scheme to distinguish actions within and across segments, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Structured text conditioning ‣ 3 Model Architecture ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>(b). Each segment’s text tokens are divided into a descriptive <em id="S3.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">head</em> for the segment’s environment and action <em id="S3.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">tails</em> <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{0},\ldots,a_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{0},\ldots,a_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, each specifying an individual action and its corresponding temporal window.
This masking scheme addresses the two aforementioned issues as follows:</p>
<ol id="S3.I2" class="ltx_enumerate" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:15pt;">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Within-segment action alignment.</span> Query tokens within an action window are restricted to attending only to the associated text tokens and the descriptive head tokens from the same segment. This preserves environmental context while reducing action-order errors and premature action execution.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cross-segment action isolation.</span> Descriptive heads remain accessible to the current and subsequent segments, whereas action tails are restricted to their originating segment. This preserves environmental context across segments while blocking access to past action descriptions, reducing action repetition in later segments.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Applying action-aware causal attention during the later training stages substantially reduces action-order errors and cross-segment action repetition.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Camera-Trajectory Conditioning</h3>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Camera trajectory encoding and injection.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hy-Nomas supports continuous camera control during
segment-wise autoregressive generation. For each segment,
given camera-to-world poses <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, we encode frame-to-frame
relative motion as <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta P_{t}=P_{t-1}^{-1}P_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta P_{t}=P_{t-1}^{-1}P_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>,
with the first increment set to the identity.
Relative transformations are computed independently within
each segment, avoiding dependence on the global coordinate
frame and camera poses from preceding segments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Frame-to-frame translations are normalized by a single video-level scale, defined as the 99th percentile of translation magnitudes across all frames. This limits the influence of extreme values on the normalization scale while preserving relative motion speeds. We pad the beginning of the camera sequence by repeating its first transformation until the sequence length is divisible by four. Each group of four consecutive <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\times 4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 4</annotation></semantics></math> transformation matrices is then flattened into a 64-dimensional vector and processed by a linear projection followed by a residual MLP, yielding one camera token per VAE latent frame. In each MMDiT block, visual tokens attend to temporally aligned camera tokens within the same segment through cross-attention:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{V}=V+\operatorname{CrossAttn}(V,C)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>V</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>CrossAttn</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{V}=V+\operatorname{CrossAttn}(V,C).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the visual tokens, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the temporally aligned camera tokens within the same segment. In cross-attention, visual tokens serve as queries, while camera tokens provide keys and values. Recent interactive world models instead rely on coarser action interfaces: some quantize both camera translation and rotation into fixed directional commands <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib95" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mao et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Happy Oyster Team, 2026</a>)</cite>, while others keep rotation continuous but restrict translation to discrete keyboard actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib97" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">Robbyant Team et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Our relative-pose trajectory keeps both translation and rotation continuous, enabling finer-grained control over direction, speed, and scale.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Segment-wise mixed-control training.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To support interleaved camera and text control during inference, we randomly disable camera conditioning on a per-segment basis during training, exposing the model to alternation between camera- and text-controlled segments. For segments with camera conditioning enabled, we remove camera descriptions from video caption to prevent the model from using them as shortcuts during training. For segments without camera conditioning, we retain these descriptions to enable text-driven camera control.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">From keyboard inputs to camera trajectories.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At inference, keyboard inputs are converted into camera trajectories. <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">W</span>/<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">S</span> control forward and backward motion, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">A</span>/<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">D</span> control lateral motion, and mouse or arrow-key inputs control yaw and pitch rotations. These translation and rotation increments are accumulated frame by frame to construct camera-to-world poses. Motion speed, scale and duration can be adjusted without retraining.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Training Infrastructure</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To efficiently process long, variable-length videos when adapting a pretrained video generator into an interactive world model through multi-stage training, we optimize distributed parallelism, data loading, and memory usage. This section describes the detailed infrastructure optimizations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Model and Data Parallelism</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training long, token-packed video sequences requires distributing both model state and activation computation across multiple GPUs. We combine Ulysses-style sequence parallelism (SP) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jacobs et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, data parallelism (DP), and FSDP2 hybrid sharding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">PyTorch Contributors, </a>)</cite>. Sequence parallelism partitions a single packed sample across a small group of GPUs, data parallelism assigns different packed samples to different groups, and FSDP2 shards model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states within each group. This organization enables sequences of up to 360K tokens while keeping parameter-sharding and sequence-parallel communication localized to small groups. On top of this parallel layout, we use a mask-flexible attention kernel for the heterogeneous segment- and action-aware masks, FLOPs-balanced sequence packing, a distributed Muon optimizer, and asynchronous checkpointing, which together determine the end-to-end throughput and robustness of long-running jobs.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sequence parallelism.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt Ulysses sequence parallelism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jacobs et al., 2023</a>)</cite> with <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\mathrm{SP}}=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>SP</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\mathrm{SP}}=8</annotation></semantics></math> to reduce activation memory for packed video and text sequences of up to 360K tokens. Both video and text tokens are partitioned along the sequence dimension across eight GPUs, with each rank holding approximately 45K tokens at maximum sequence length. During attention, an all-to-all collective transforms sequence shards into head shards, allowing each rank to compute a subset of attention heads over the full sequence, followed by a reverse all-to-all to restore sequence sharding for local normalization, residual, and MLP operations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data parallelism.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each eight-GPU SP group forms one logical data-parallel replica and processes a different packed batch. For <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\mathrm{GPU}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>GPU</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\mathrm{GPU}}</annotation></semantics></math> total GPUs and sequence-parallel degree <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\mathrm{SP}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>SP</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\mathrm{SP}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the number of replicas is <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\mathrm{DP}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{GPU}}}{N_{\mathrm{SP}}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>DP</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>GPU</mi></msub><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>SP</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\mathrm{DP}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{GPU}}}{N_{\mathrm{SP}}}.</annotation></semantics></math> The precomputed packing plan assigns a different pack to each replica, while gradients are synchronized across replicas to maintain a consistent global model update. Because the gradient synchronization waits for the slowest replica, the packs are balanced by their estimated FLOPs rather than by sample count or token count (see Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Training Throughput Optimization ‣ 4 Training Infrastructure ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>), reducing workload variation caused by differences in video resolution, duration, and mask density.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">FSDP2 hybrid sharding.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ FSDP2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">PyTorch Contributors, </a>)</cite> with a logical distributed mesh organized as</p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\text{DP replication},\ \text{DP sharding},\ \text{sequence parallelism}]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mtext>DP replication</mtext><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mtext>DP sharding</mtext><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mtext>sequence parallelism</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\text{DP replication},\ \text{DP sharding},\ \text{sequence parallelism}].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The explicit DP-shard size is set to one. In our implementation, the DP-shard and SP dimensions are combined when constructing the FSDP shard group. Consequently, parameters, gradients, and optimizer states are effectively sharded across the same eight GPUs that form one SP group, and the resulting model shard is replicated across the data-parallel groups.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This topology avoids performing parameter all-gathers and gradient reduce-scatters over the entire job. These collectives remain within the eight-GPU shard group, while gradient synchronization across replicated groups provides global data-parallel scaling. Parameter all-gathers and gradient reduce-scatters are overlapped with forward and backward computation whenever their dependencies permit. The design therefore trades local communication for substantial reductions in per-GPU model-state memory.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>GPU Memory Optimization</h3>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Activation checkpointing.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All main transformer blocks use activation checkpointing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2016</a>)</cite>. Standard checkpointing stores the block input during the forward pass and reconstructs intermediate activations during backpropagation, requiring both the attention and MLP computations to be executed again. Following the principle of selective activation checkpointing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">PyTorch Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, we additionally support selective recomputation through <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">skip_attn_recompute</span>. When enabled, the attention output and required softmax statistics are retained from the original forward pass. Backward recomputation reuses these saved attention results and recomputes only the remaining block operations, including the MLP. This option preserves attention gradients while avoiding a second execution of the attention forward kernel, trading additional activation memory for lower recomputation cost.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Stage-dependent memory strategy.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The optimal memory policy depends on the training algorithm. During one-shot training, particularly after the introduction of per-layer camera attention, we enable selective attention checkpointing, asynchronous activation offload, and camera-module checkpointing. Saved attention outputs and checkpoint inputs can be transferred to pinned CPU memory, reducing GPU memory pressure while preserving the compute savings from skipping attention recomputation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">During segment forcing, we instead disable attention-output retention and activation offload. Segment-wise streaming backward already bounds peak memory by releasing intermediate activations as the serial rollout progresses. In this regime, retaining attention outputs increased memory by approximately 1.6 GB per rank without providing a meaningful speed improvement. We therefore use ordinary attention recomputation together with streaming backward.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Training Throughput Optimization</h3>

<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">FLOPs-based sequence packing.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To improve training throughput on long videos with varying spatial resolutions and durations, we employ sequence packing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krell et al., 2022</a>)</cite> to combine 480p and 720p videos spanning 5–75 seconds into token-budgeted batches. Packing preserves each token’s sample identity and original spatial, temporal, and segment metadata, with block-diagonal attention preventing information leaking across videos. Conditioning signals are packed with video tokens to preserve text–segment and camera–frame alignment, while the training loss is computed only over valid video tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Balancing token counts alone does not ensure balanced computation, as segment-wise causal attention incurs substantially different costs depending on the number of unmasked query–key pairs. We therefore estimate the computational cost of each sample directly. Let <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the number of valid video and text tokens of sample <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, and let</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i}=\sum_{p\in i}\bigl|\{q:M^{(i)}_{pq}\neq-\infty\}\bigr|" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">|</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>≠</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i}=\sum_{p\in i}\bigl|\{q:M^{(i)}_{pq}\neq-\infty\}\bigr|</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">denote the number of unmasked query–key pairs under its segment- and action-aware mask <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>. For segment lengths <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{1},\ldots,m_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>S</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{1},\ldots,m_{S}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is dominated by <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{j=1}^{S}m_{j}\sum_{k\leq j}m_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>S</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{j=1}^{S}m_{j}\sum_{k\leq j}m_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, which can be computed from segment metadata without materializing the mask. We model the estimated per-sample training FLOPs as</p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{i}=\alpha n_{i}+\beta A_{i}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{i}=\alpha n_{i}+\beta A_{i},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> captures the per-token cost of linear operations across the 54 blocks, including camera cross-attention, and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> captures the per-pair cost of <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="QK^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">QK^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="PV" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">PV</annotation></semantics></math> operations. Both coefficients account for backward propagation and activation recomputation, and are derived analytically from the architecture in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Model Architecture ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and calibrated against measured step times.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We construct the packing plan offline in two stages. First, samples are grouped into packs satisfying the token budget <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i\in\mathrm{pack}}n_{i}\leq N_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>pack</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i\in\mathrm{pack}}n_{i}\leq N_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>, while targeting similar estimated FLOPs per pack. Second, packs are assigned to the <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\mathrm{DP}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>DP</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\mathrm{DP}}</annotation></semantics></math> replicas using a longest-processing-time-first greedy algorithm, sorting packs by estimated FLOPs in descending order and assigning each to the least-loaded replica. This balances computational workloads across replicas and reduces synchronization-induced idle time. The resulting plan is stored alongside the data index and loaded by the dataloader without additional runtime scheduling overhead, with consistent packing assignments across ranks within each sequence-parallel group.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Efficient attention with structured masks.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our training combines segment-causal and action-aware attention with block-diagonal boundaries across packed videos, resulting in complex attention masks over sequences of up to 360K tokens. Dense masks are prohibitively expensive at this scale, while standard FlashAttention kernels <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib94" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shah et al., 2024</a>)</cite> cannot efficiently handle such irregular attention patterns. We therefore adopt the Flex-Flash-Attention (FFA) kernel from MagiAttention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib92" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tao and Huang, 2025</a>)</cite>, which represents structured masks as compact attention slices and skips masked attention blocks. We construct these slices directly from sample, segment, and action metadata without materializing dense masks. We further integrate FFA with eight-way Ulysses sequence parallelism, where each rank processes two of the 16 attention heads over the packed sequence using the same slice specification. This avoids the repeated key–value communication of context-parallel approaches while retaining only two all-to-all collectives per attention layer.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Distributed Muon optimizer.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train the DiT using Muon <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jordan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> for the weight matrices in attention and feed-forward layers, and AdamW <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib134" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019</a>)</cite> for embeddings, biases, and other remaining parameters. To support Muon’s full-matrix orthogonalization under FSDP2 parameter sharding, we adopt the distributed Muon implementation from Canzona <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Asynchronous checkpointing and deterministic resumption.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We build upon ByteCheckpoint <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib91" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to asynchronously save FSDP2-sharded model and optimizer states, overlapping serialization and storage I/O with training through pinned CPU memory. To ensure deterministic resumption, we additionally checkpoint all dataloader states, including packing-plan positions and sampler states, together with all CPU and GPU RNG states. Restoring these states preserves data ordering and stochastic operations across training interruptions. Furthermore, our global tensor metadata enables checkpoint resharding across different GPU counts and parallel configurations without offline conversion.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Model Training</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We progressively adapt a pretrained bidirectional DiT into an interactive world model through coordinated curricula in causality, interaction, and context length. Section <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Training Curriculum ‣ 5 Model Training ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a> explains the design of this progression, and Sections <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Continual Pre-Training ‣ 5 Model Training ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>–<a href="#S5.SS5" title="5.5 Diffusion Distillation ‣ 5 Model Training ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.5</span></a> describe its implementation, from continual pre-training to few-step autoregressive generation. Section <a href="#S5.SS6" title="5.6 Downstream Adaptation via LoRA ‣ 5 Model Training ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a> presents a lightweight recipe for downstream adaptation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Training Curriculum</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our training strategy introduces each capability on top of an already learned foundation. Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Context curriculum. ‣ 5.1 Training Curriculum ‣ 5 Model Training ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes the five stages, with continual pre-training (CPT) divided into three successive regimes. Together, these stages advance three complementary curricula.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Causal curriculum.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We progress from <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">segment-wise causal attention</em> to <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">action-aware causal attention</em>, followed by <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">segment forcing</em> and <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">diffusion distillation</em>. Segment-wise masking first establishes the information flow required for autoregressive generation: each segment uses its current instruction and preceding history, while attention remains bidirectional within the segment. Action-aware masking then refines this structure by setting bounded temporal scope for each action instruction, addressing action-order errors and the repetition of earlier actions. Segment forcing subsequently trains the model with cached context from its own predictions, exposing the model to imperfect histories before inference. Finally, causal distillation reduces the sampling steps while further mitigating error accumulation due to training and inference mismatch. This curriculum progressively convert a bidirectional DiT into an efficient autoregressive model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Interaction curriculum.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We extend a <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">bidirectional, noninteractive text-to-video DiT</em> into a model supporting <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">multi-turn free-form text interaction</em>, and then <em id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">free-form text interaction with continuous camera control</em>. Segment-wise captions and causal attention teach the model to respond to successive text instructions while carrying forward relevant visual context. Camera-conditioned CPT adds geometric control capabilities after the foundation for text-prompt interaction has been established. Mixing text-only and camera-conditioned segments, together with segment-wise camera dropout, exposes the model to transitions between different interaction modes within a sequence. The resulting model can continue an evolving world under either semantic instructions or explicit camera motion.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Context curriculum.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We combine mixed-resolution and mixed-length training with a progressive increase in the maximum packed sequence length. The context length is set to <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="180K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>180</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">180K</annotation></semantics></math> tokens before action-aware CPT and increases to <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="360K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>360</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">360K</annotation></semantics></math> tokens from action-aware CPT onward. Mixing resolutions and durations balances spatial detail and temporal coverage; expanding the context length helps the model to understand longer histories and generate richer instruction video sequences. Sequence packing and memory optimizations in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Training Infrastructure ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> make this progression practical. A context length of <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="360K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>360</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">360K</annotation></semantics></math> tokens is sufficient to generate minute-scale visual worlds at <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="720p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>720</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">720p</annotation></semantics></math> resolution.</p>
</div>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Continual Pre-Training</h3>

<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Latent-space adaptation.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We initialize  Hy-Nomas from HunyuanVideo 1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and adapt its VAE to DCAE-V <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, increasing spatial compression from <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32\times 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32\times 32</annotation></semantics></math> while keeping temporal compression as a factor of four. This significantly reduces the latent token count at a given video resolution and duration, making training on longer sequences more feasible. We first freeze the intermediate DiT blocks and update only the input projection and output layers for 20K steps, then train the full DiT for another 60K steps.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">From segment causality to action alignment.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CPT first establishes segment-wise causal attention on diverse, variable-length videos with dense structured captions, then continues with higher-quality data under the same attention structure. We subsequently introduce action-aware masking with temporally localized annotations. The key transition is to supervise <em id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">when</em> an instruction applies: descriptive context remains available across segments, whereas action instructions are restricted to their originating segment and annotated temporal windows. Increasing the context length at this stage allows training to include longer action sequences and histories. The attention design is specified in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Segment-wise Causal Attention ‣ 3 Model Architecture ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Camera control.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At the end of CPT, we introduce the camera-control interaction capability. Normalized camera extrinsics are encoded as one token per latent frame and injected through frame-wise cross-attention after every MMDiT block. Both the base DiT and the camera modules remain trainable, allowing camera control to be learned jointly with visual quality and prompt adherence. During this training stage, both the camera trajectory and camera-related text descriptions are dropped with <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math> probability for each segment. This allows camera-control interaction and text-prompt interaction to coexist within the same video while preventing text-based camera descriptions in captions from leaking the camera motion.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>High-Quality Annealing</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After broad capability acquisition, we anneal on high-quality, predominantly single-subject videos from various targeted sources. Kimi K3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moonshot AI, 2026</a>)</cite> is used to generate more accurate dense captions, and we increase the maximum text length from 768 to 1,280 tokens to accommodate more detailed segment descriptions and longer action sequences. The model architecture and flow-matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2023</a>)</cite> objective remain unchanged.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use different supervision for annealing data according to its camera trajectory quality. Videos whose ViPE trajectories pass validity and motion-variance filters enter the camera-conditioned path; those with unreliable trajectories remain useful as text-conditioned training samples. Camera trajectories are normalized with a shared video-level scale preserving relative motion magnitudes across segments. This concentrates learning on precise text and camera motion supervision while retaining useful videos that lack reliable camera trajectories.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Segment Forcing</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Segment Forcing adapts the model to the evolving history it consumes during autoregressive inference. Inspired by training with model-generated context in Self Forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, we combine sequential segment-wise denoising, one-step context estimation, and streaming backward. This exposes later segments to prediction errors while retaining direct flow-matching supervision for each current segment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given a video divided into multiple segments, the autoregressive DiT processes the segments sequentially. At segment <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, the model takes the noisy latent <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{s,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{s,t}</annotation></semantics></math> as input and predicts its flow-matching velocity <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>, conditioned on the KV cache constructed from preceding segments and prompts. We apply the flow-matching MSE objective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2023</a>)</cite> only to the current segment prediction. The resulting loss is immediately backpropagated, after which the computation graph and intermediate activations of the current segment are released to save GPU memory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To construct the context for the next segment, we perform one-step denoising from the same noisy latent <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{s,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{s,t}</annotation></semantics></math> using the predicted velocity:</p>
<table id="S5.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{s,t_{\mathrm{ctx}}}=\mathbf{x}_{s,t}+(t_{\mathrm{ctx}}-t)\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{s},\qquad t_{\mathrm{ctx}}\sim\mathcal{U}(0.1,0.3)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>ctx</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>ctx</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>ctx</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{s,t_{\mathrm{ctx}}}=\mathbf{x}_{s,t}+(t_{\mathrm{ctx}}-t)\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{s},\qquad t_{\mathrm{ctx}}\sim\mathcal{U}(0.1,0.3).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.2" class="ltx_p">The sampled range approximates the noise levels of context segments encountered during autoregressive inference. The resulting low-noise latent is appended to the KV cache and used as context for subsequent segments. We omit this cache update for the final segment because no later segment consumes it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">By repeatedly generating and caching its own context, the model is trained under a history distribution that closely matches autoregressive inference. Meanwhile, streaming backward keeps only the latest segment’s computation graph in memory. Gradients are accumulated across segments, followed by a single optimizer step after the full sequence has been processed. The complete pipeline is illustrated in Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5.4 Segment Forcing ‣ 5 Model Training ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.36729v1/segment_self_forcing_streaming_backward_paper.svg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/169;" width="476" height="169"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span><span id="S5.F7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Segment Forcing with streaming backward.</span> Each current segment receives a flow-matching loss; a one-step low-noise estimation supplies cached context for later segments. Streaming backward retains only one segment’s computation graph at a time, accumulating gradients for a single optimizer step after the full sequence. The cache update of the final segment is skipped.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Diffusion Distillation</h3>

<section id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Causal distillation.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Starting from the AR model trained with segment self-forcing, we use two-stage distillation to reduce the sampling budget from 100 to 4 network function evaluations (NFEs) per segment. The two stages establish few-step generation and then refine visual fidelity and motion stability while preserving semantic alignment and camera controllability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Stage I: Few-Step Initialization.</span>
Drawing on consistency-based distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we initialize the student with a causal adaptation of Phased Consistency Models (PCM). The teacher’s denoising trajectory is partitioned into phases, and the student learns to map noisy states within each phase to its lower boundary. Training uses teacher forcing: each segment is conditioned on ground-truth history, text, and camera inputs. The resulting few-step checkpoint initializes Stage II.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Stage II: Quality Refinement.</span>
Starting from the PCM checkpoint, we refine the student under hybrid forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to improve visual fidelity and motion stability while preserving semantic alignment. For longer sequences, a noise-perturbed ground-truth prefix initializes the student’s causal KV cache. The student then generates the suffix autoregressively with 4 NFEs per segment, using each generated segment as context for the next. This combines ground-truth context with training on the student’s own generated history. Shorter sequences are generated entirely by the student.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We jointly optimize the student with a causal adaptation of Decoupled Distribution Matching Distillation (DDMD) and an adversarial hinge objective, drawing on distribution-matching distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> and adversarial distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sauer et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2026a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>, respectively. DDMD samples noise levels independently for CFG and DM, restricting CFG to the remaining denoising interval while sampling DM over the full interval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. DDMD supervision is applied only to the final generated segment, with gradients stopped through earlier segments and their cached representations. The teacher remains frozen, while the fake-score model is trained with flow matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2023</a>)</cite> on detached student samples. The adversarial objective complements DDMD with supervision from high-quality real videos to improve visual fidelity and motion stability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Causal inference.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At inference, the distilled student generates segments autoregressively with 4 NFEs per segment, conditioned on text, camera inputs, and previously generated history. After each segment is generated, we perturb it with flow noise at <math id="S5.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.206897" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.206897</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.206897</annotation></semantics></math> before updating the causal KV cache for subsequent segments.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.6 </span>Downstream Adaptation via LoRA</h3>

style="--ltx-stroke-color:#168876;" stroke="#168876" stroke-width="0.9pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 414.01 0 L 459.49 0"></path><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#168876;" fill="#168876" stroke-dasharray="none" stroke-dashoffset="0.0pt" stroke-linejoin="miter" stroke-width="0.84375pt" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 457.03 0)"><path d="M 5.36 0 L 1.88 1.28 L 2.75 0 L 1.88 -1.28 Z"></path></g></g></g></g></svg></span>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span><span id="S5.F8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Downstream LoRA adaptation workflow.</span> Train LoRA adapters
on the base autoregressive model (before distillation), then merge the learned weights into
the distilled model for efficient deployment, without
full-model fine-tuning or repeating distillation.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To help users customize our model for their use cases, we provide a recommended workflow based on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. We present this workflow as our best-practice recipe for downstream adaptation and encourage users to follow it when developing their own specialized models.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Best practices for downstream adaptation.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We recommend training LoRA adapters on the base autoregressive model before distillation, then merging the learned LoRA adapter weights into the distilled model for deployment. The workflow is illustrated in Figure <a href="#S5.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 5.6 Downstream Adaptation via LoRA ‣ 5 Model Training ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. Users can follow this recipe with on the order of 100 task-specific samples selected to reflect their intended visual style, usage scenario, or application domain. This workflow enables lightweight customization without full-model fine-tuning or repeating the distillation pipeline, while retaining the inference efficiency of the distilled model. The following examples illustrate these best practices and provide practical references for users adapting the model to their own applications.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cinematic style LoRA.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As an example of visual-style adaptation, we train a cinematic-style LoRA adapter on the base autoregressive model using cinematic videos paired with high-quality captions from K3 as our SFT data. We set the LoRA rank to 256 and alpha to 512, and train for 500 iterations with a learning rate of <math id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>. For effective domain adaptation, we recommend using a slightly higher learning rate than that used for base-model training. Due to the small size of the SFT dataset, we employ sequence packing in the data loader such that each training iteration covers the entire dataset, making 500 iterations equivalent to 500 epochs. We then merge the resulting LoRA adapter weights into the distilled model for inference.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Robotics LoRA.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond visual-style adaptation, robotics is another potential application of this recipe. We perform task-specific robotics LoRA fine-tuning on a set of robotics dual-arm egocentric task videos <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">RealSource, 2025</a>)</cite>, which is not overlapped with our training set. We conduct the LoRA tuning for approximately <math id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1,500" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1,500</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1,500</annotation></semantics></math> epochs on the selected 128-sample tuning set with a LoRA rank of 512.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In Section <a href="#S7.SS4" title="7.4 LoRA Adaption Results ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7.4</span></a>, we provide a preliminary evaluation of the LoRA-adapted model against the distilled model before merging the LoRA weights.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Model Inference</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Interactive deployment requires translating user intent into suitable conditioning inputs and generating responses efficiently. To address these complementary requirements, we develop a VLM-based Prompt Enhancer (PE) and optimize the model’s inference pipeline.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The PE translates user intent into structured instructions for the video generator. Given previously generated video segments, the current user instruction, and optional camera-control signals, the PE produces a prompt for the next segment. This design builds on recent approaches to streaming text control and agent-mediated world interaction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang and others, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>, while using a structured caption format aligned with our training annotations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Prompt Enhancer</h3>
