<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span><span id="S6.F9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompt Enhancer (PE) workflow</span>. PE generates an initial dense caption in the first turn. In subsequent turns, users can choose text prompts or camera control, and PE combines the selected input with the full interaction history to generate a dense caption that AR-DiT uses to produce the next video segment. Each turn’s dialogue and generated video are appended to the history.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.1.1 </span>Prompt Enhancer Workflow</h4>

<section id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multi-turn interaction.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prompt Enhancer (PE) converts user instructions into structured dense captions for
segment-by-segment video generation. At each turn, PE produces one caption
for the next segment, which the DiT then uses to generate the corresponding
video. The interaction proceeds causally: each new turn conditions on the
current user input and the complete history accumulated so far.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Formally, the caption at turn <math id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is generated as</p>
<table id="S6.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S6.E8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="y_{t}\sim p_{\theta}\!\left(\cdot\mid S,u_{t},H_{t-1},V_{&lt;t},m_{t}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}\sim p_{\theta}\!\left(\cdot\mid S,u_{t},H_{t-1},V_{&lt;t},m_{t}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is the system prompt, <math id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the current user input, and <math id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>
specifies the rewriting mode. The dialogue history <math id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> contains
all preceding user requests and PE responses, while
<math id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{&lt;t}=(V_{1},\ldots,V_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{&lt;t}=(V_{1},\ldots,V_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math> contains all previously generated video
segments. Both histories are empty at the first turn. After each round,
the dialogue and generated video are retained as context for subsequent
turns.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Initial and incremental captions.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The output format depends on the turn and the selected control mode:</p>
<ul id="S6.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:10pt;">
<li id="S6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">First-turn initialization.</span>
The user provides subject and environment descriptions, together with
any specified visual style and viewing perspective. PE returns
video-level metadata and the first segment caption, including
<span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">visual_description_long</span> to establish the scene and
<span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">contained_actions</span> to specify subject actions, according to the caption format defined in Figure <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Multi-turn annotation ‣ 2.4 Video Captioning ‣ 2 Data ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Subsequent turns in text prompt mode.</span>
PE combines the current user description with the full dialogue and
video history to produce an incremental dense caption. The output
contains <span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">description_change</span> for scene and camera updates
relative to the established context, and <span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">contained_actions</span>
for the next segment’s subject behavior.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Subsequent turns in camera control mode.</span>
PE outputs only <span id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">description_change</span>, leaving
<span id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">contained_actions</span> empty. The user-defined camera trajectory
is supplied separately to DiT alongside this incremental caption.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">6.1.2 </span>Prompt Enhancer Training</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To support local deployment, we train a lightweight PE model using a dataset of multi-turn multimodal conversations. Each turn pairs the current user instruction and previous dialogue and video history with a structured dense caption response. We construct the data in two ways. First, we synthesize user prompts from existing dense captions, checking that the prompts preserve the specified subject attributes, scene content, and action ordering. Second, we collect real user prompts as seed data and augment them into more synthetic user prompts. We then run these user prompts through the complete PE and video generation pipeline, recording the caption response and generated video at each turn. Each PE turn uses the current instruction and the full dialogue and video history from previous turns. The dataset includes scene initialization and follow-up interactions across different subjects, environments, viewpoints, and control modes. We also add examples to expand the coverage of action types, different action combinations, and temporal orderings, and check for inconsistencies between instructions, captions, and successive segments.
We use Qwen3.8-27B as our base model and train our PE through supervised fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Inference Optimization</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To make our model accessible to users with limited GPU resources, we optimize both autoregres-
sive generation and video decoding for deployment on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. We com-
bine INT8 storage, sliding-window attention (SWA), and CPU offloading to reduce GPU memory
usage, and use sparse attention to improve generation efficiency. For video decoding, we train
a PixelDiT decoder based on PixelUMM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and optimize it for single-GPU inference.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Efficient single-GPU inference on NVIDIA RTX 4090.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We reduce inference memory primarily through INT8 quantization, sliding-window attention (SWA), and CPU offloading. We quantize model weights and cache historical attention keys and values in INT8 with floating-point scales, dequantizing them to BF16 during computation while keeping the current segment’s attention inputs in BF16. SWA maintains a bounded history on the GPU, preventing the KV cache from growing with rollout duration. We further offload inactive model components to CPU memory between pipeline stages, such as offloading the VAE during DiT denoising and loading the text encoder only when needed. This reduces peak memory usage at the cost of CPU–GPU transfer latency. Peak GPU memory also depends on the current segment length and temporary computation buffers. For example, generating a 100-second video across seven segments at 1280<math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>704 resolution and 24 FPS requires 20.53 GiB of peak GPU memory. To further accelerate inference, we use dense attention for the first two denoising steps, followed by sparse attention that retains 25% of candidate video blocks in subsequent steps. These optimizations may introduce subtle differences that become more noticeable over successive segments during autoregressive generation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">PixelUMM decoder adaptation.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We replace the DCAE-V decoder with a pixel-space diffusion decoder initialized from the vision part of PixelUMM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. The decoder takes the DCAE-V latents as a condition and recovers the corresponding video from pixel-space Gaussian noise. When reconstructing videos with complex natural textures, the original DCAE-V decoder, which operates on highly compressed latents, tends to output a repetitive grid-like pattern in place of the true texture. In contrast, our decoder uses its pretrained generative prior to restore realistic high-frequency details. The decoder is trained with PixelUMM’s diffusion loss, first on images and 40-frame videos at <math id="S6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256\times 256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>256</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256\times 256</annotation></semantics></math>, and then on images and longer videos at 384p–720p. For long videos, we adopt the temporal tiling strategy of the H3 decoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">MiniMax, 2026</a>)</cite> rather than that of the DCAE-V decoder, decoding overlapping chunks of 40 frames with a 20-frame overlap blended by cosine weights. Spatially, instead of overlapping tiling, which incurs substantial redundant computation, we decode each frame in a single pass and use sliding-tile attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, in which each patch attends only to the patches in a local spatial neighborhood across all frames in the chunk. Finally, we distill the decoder with DMD2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> for one-step inference, and accelerate its inference on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with FP8 quantization.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Evaluation</h2>

<figure id="S7.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.36729v1/Hy-Nomas-Bench_overview_clear.png" id="S7.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/250;" width="476" height="250" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span><span id="S7.F10.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Overview of Hy-Nomas-Bench.</span>
<span id="S7.F10.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top:</span> Model outputs for an example case from Bench-3 (interleaved text–camera control).
<span id="S7.F10.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bottom:</span> (a) World settings span diverse scenes, visual styles,
subjects, and viewpoints. (b) 280 cases cover multi-turn text interaction, camera navigation,
interleaved control, and spatial memory.
(c) Unified control maps instructions to text, binary key states
<math id="S7.F10.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[T,8]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[T,8]</annotation></semantics></math> (<span id="S7.F10.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">W/A/S/D</span> and four arrow keys), or per-frame
<math id="S7.F10.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\times 4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 4</annotation></semantics></math> camera-to-world matrices <math id="S7.F10.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[T,4,4]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[T,4,4]</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S7.F10.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is the
frame count. Generation continues across turns without world resets.
(d) Three annotators evaluate prompt following, physical plausibility,
camera control, and memory consistency through pairwise comparisons.
Results are summarized by win/tie/loss rates and net win rate
(win minus loss, in percentage points).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To systematically evaluate interaction capability and memory
consistency of world models, we introduce <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hy-Nomas-Bench</span>, comprising
280 test cases across four benchmarks: multi-turn text interaction,
camera navigation, interleaved text–camera control, and spatial memory. We compare  Hy-Nomas with three representative interactive world models: Genie 3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google DeepMind, 2025</a>)</cite>, LingBot-World v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>, and Happy Oyster <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Happy Oyster Team, 2026</a>)</cite>. We generate outputs using each model’s supported interaction interface and conduct pairwise human evaluation on prompt following, physical plausibility, camera control, and memory consistency.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.1 </span>Hy-Nomas-Bench and Metrics</h3>

<div id="S7.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The overview of Hy-Nomas-Bench is shown in
Figure <a href="#S7.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>. We construct four benchmarks totaling 280 test cases
that assess model capabilities through free-form text prompts, keyboard-based camera commands, and interleaved text and camera inputs, as well as spatial memory across successive interactions. The benchmarks cover first-person, second-person, third-person following, and third-person observer viewpoints in photorealistic, game-like, and animated environments. We release original user prompts for evaluating other models through their native interfaces, alongside PE-enhanced prompts following our structured caption format to reproduce our results <span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://huggingface.co/datasets/tencent/Hy-Nomas-Bench" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/datasets/tencent/Hy-Nomas-Bench</a></span></span></span>. Camera controls provide frame-aligned keyboard states and reference poses with explicit timing and motion conventions. All four benchmarks cover complex multi-turn interactions with cases that require the model to generate videos longer than <math id="S7.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>60</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60</annotation></semantics></math> seconds.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We consider four dimensions to evaluate world models. <span id="S7.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Prompt following</span> measures adherence to free-form text instructions; <span id="S7.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">physical plausibility</span> assesses the realism and consistency of generated physical interactions; <span id="S7.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">camera control</span> measures how accurately the model responds to navigation commands; and <span id="S7.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">memory consistency</span> assesses spatial coherence when revisiting previously observed environments. These criteria are designed to cover different capabilities of world models, <em id="S7.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">i.e</em>.<span id="S7.SS1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text"></span>, instruction execution, plausible dynamics, navigation, and spatial recall. Conventional evaluation metrics used in video generation are not considered in Hy-Nomas-Bench (such as visual fidelity, aesthetics, audio quality, <em id="S7.SS1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">etc</em>.<span id="S7.SS1.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text"></span>), as we focus on capabilities that are crucial to world models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A closely related work is WBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib103" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ying et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, which evaluates text-prompt and camera-control capability separately, since most existing models can only handle one type of interaction. In contrast, we introduce interleaved text and camera control within a single continuous test case. We also assess spatial memory through specially designed camera trajectories that leave and return to an earlier viewpoint, testing whether previously observed anchor objects and environments remain present and consistent. We describe each benchmark below.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bench-1: Multi-turn free-form text.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark examines whether instruction execution remains consistent with an evolving scene across successive turns. We construct 60 scenarios with 2–6 turns, using prompts curated by human annotators. The sequences include interactions that depend on entities and states established in preceding turns, requiring models to execute new instructions while retaining relevant scene context. This introduces dependencies across turns beyond isolated action completion: previously introduced subjects must remain identifiable, object interactions must remain compatible with the current scene, and action transitions must remain physically plausible. The resulting sequences probe both local instruction adherence and the persistence of scene content throughout the whole video.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bench-2: Camera navigation.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark targets the combination of different keyboard actions and reversibility of camera controls. The 100 cases cover all eight basic keyboard actions and all 24 two-key combinations that exclude opposing inputs along the same control axis. These combinations encompass simultaneous translations, simultaneous rotations, and coupled translation–rotation motions, testing whether individually meaningful controls remain correctly composed when applied together. Each segment holds a fixed action for 2–4 seconds and is followed by an equal-duration inverse action. Under the specified motion-integration rules, the reference trajectories return to the same position and orientation at each pair boundary. This construction provides controlled motion intervals and known return poses for examining directional adherence, coupled-motion errors, and drift over successive outbound–return pairs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bench-3: Interleaved text and camera control.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark tests whether control responsiveness and scene continuity persist when switching between text prompts and camera control within a rollout. The 60 cases contain 2–7 segments, each specifying either a free-form semantic interaction or an explicit camera-control sequence. Bench-3 covers both text-to-camera and camera-to-text transitions. Text segments introduce actions and scene changes, while camera segments navigate the scene under prescribed camera trajectories. It requires models to preserve the consequences of earlier interactions during navigation and interpret subsequent text instructions correctly to update the scene. World models need to respond correctly when switching between different control signals.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bench-4: Spatial memory.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark evaluates whether previously observed content remains consistent after leaving the field of view. We construct 60 first-person scenarios, evenly distributed across real-world and game-style indoor and outdoor environments. Each scenario contains a distinctive static anchor object and eight camera-control segments forming four outbound–return pairs, covering translations, rotations, and more complex camera motions. A static anchor object is used as a reference to identify any memory inconsistency. The camera trajectories are designed to take the anchor out of view before returning to a previously observed viewpoint. The task of Bench-4 is to compare initial and revisited frames at matched camera positions and orientations, and assess the differences between the frames. We focus on the anchor’s identity and appearance, as well as the surrounding scene layout when measuring memory consistency. Figure <a href="#S7.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ Bench-4: Spatial memory. ‣ 7.1 Hy-Nomas-Bench and Metrics ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> illustrates the anchor-based camera trajectory designs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.36729v1/Hy-Nomas-Bench4_indoor.png" id="S7.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/208;" width="429" height="208" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span><span id="S7.F11.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Illustration of the design of Bench-4: Spatial memory.</span>
Each uses a static
anchor object and four outbound–return pairs. Bench-4
evaluates object permanence under different camera movements, and appearance/layout consistency.
<span id="S7.F11.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left:</span> Different trajectory types.
<span id="S7.F11.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Center:</span> Scene, camera frustum, and trajectory.
<span id="S7.F11.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right:</span> Inference results by  Hy-Nomas.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.2 </span>Evaluation Protocol</h3>

<section id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation setup.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate different models with heterogeneous interaction interfaces, we adapt Hy-Nomas-Bench to each model’s native interaction setting while preserving the designed task within each benchmark. Models that require an initial image are initialized with the first frame generated by Hy-Nomas, ensuring a consistent visual starting point. Unless stated otherwise, all models are evaluated at their original resolutions using their default inference settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Hy-Nomas supports interleaved text and camera control within one unified model. For LingBot-World v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>, we adapt their open-source model for free-form text and interleaved evaluation. Genie 3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google DeepMind, 2025</a>)</cite> is only evaluated on camera navigation and spatial memory, as the official API does not support text-prompt based interactions. Happy Oyster <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Happy Oyster Team, 2026</a>)</cite> is evaluated separately in <em id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Directing</em> mode for text interaction and <em id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Wandering</em> mode for navigation, and it does not support interleaved text and camera control within the same video. Table <a href="#S7.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Evaluation setup. ‣ 7.2 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> summarizes the evaluation settings across different models. Due to the interaction limitations of each model, some benchmarks are not applicable to certain models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.T3" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S7.T3.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S7.T3.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S7.T3.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt">System</td>
<td id="S7.T3.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">
<span id="S7.T3.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block">
<span id="S7.T3.2.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Multi-turn</span>
<span id="S7.T3.2.1.2.1.2" class="ltx_p">free-form text</span>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span><span id="S7.F12.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qualitative comparison of multi-turn text interaction.</span>
In the first example,  Hy-Nomas clearly shows
the apple being grasped, lifted, and brought to the plate.
LingBot-World v2 changes the apple’s color and gripper structure, while
HappyOyster-Directing shows discontinuous views without a clear
grasp-and-lift progression.
In the second example,  Hy-Nomas visualizes the requested spatula, cutting on
the board, and strawberries in the glass bowl. LingBot-World v2 only shows
cutting strawberries and a knife without spatula, while
HappyOyster-Directing does not move strawberries into the bowl.
</figcaption>
</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 13: </span>
<span id="S7.F13.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pairwise human evaluation of multi-turn text control.</span>
We compare  Hy-Nomas with HappyOyster-Directing and
LingBot-World v2 on prompt following and physical plausibility.
Within each evaluation dimension, the two 100% stacked bars show wins
(green), ties (gray), and losses (pink) from the perspective of
 Hy-Nomas.

</section>
<section id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Human evaluation.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each metric of Hy-Nomas-Bench, we report pairwise win, tie, and loss percentage from the perspective of  Hy-Nomas. The net win rate is the win percentage minus the loss percentage.
Evaluations are conducted by groups of trained human annotators. Each group has three annotators, who discuss and calibrate their scoring criteria to improve consistency.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.3 </span>Comparison with Other World Models</h3>

<div id="S7.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Overall,  Hy-Nomas demonstrates superior interaction capability and supports different control signals for interaction. Notably, Genie 3 does not provide a free-form text interaction capability in its official API. Happy Oyster adopts separate models for each control signal, thus can not support text and camera interleaved interaction. Although LingBot-World v2 can cover all the settings by adapting its open-source model, it exhibits substantially weaker performance in following free-form text instructions, as its text-based control is implemented by selecting VLM-generated proposals to guide the generation of the subsequent video segment, rather than taking free-form text instructions from the user. From Bench-1 to Bench-3,  Hy-Nomas consistently achieves the best performance, highlighting both its versatility and effectiveness in handling heterogeneous control signals. Despite these advantages, spatial memory remains an area for improvement. While  Hy-Nomas performs comparably to Happy Oyster, it still trails Genie 3 in maintaining long-term spatial consistency, suggesting research opportunities to further improve  Hy-Nomas’s memory capability.
We break down the results for each benchmark below.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bench-1: Multi-turn free-form text interaction.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S7.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Evaluation setup. ‣ 7.2 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> summarizes the results. For prompt following,  Hy-Nomas achieves win rates of 65.0% against HappyOyster-Directing and 75.0% against LingBot-World v2. For physical plausibility,  Hy-Nomas achieves win rates of 45.0% and 68.3%.
These results demonstrate that  Hy-Nomas consistently outperforms both models in instruction following and physical plausibility, with stronger advantages over LingBot-World v2. We hypothesize that our structured captions and attention design contribute to these improvements by providing explicit supervision of actions, scene changes and camera movements. Figures <a href="#S7.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ Evaluation setup. ‣ 7.2 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> provides qualitative examples for multi-turn text interaction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bench-2: Camera control.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S7.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Bench-2: Camera control. ‣ 7.3 Comparison with Other World Models ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> presents the results on camera control across all four models.  Hy-Nomas consistently achieves higher win rates than loss rates against the other three models. Compared with the results on Bench-1, the advantage of  Hy-Nomas is smaller for camera control, which has been studied more widely for the world model. Figure <a href="#S7.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ Bench-2: Camera control. ‣ 7.3 Comparison with Other World Models ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> complements these results with an indoor navigation example.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 14: </span><span id="S7.F14.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qualitative comparison of camera control in an indoor scene.</span>
Rows show  Hy-Nomas (Ours), LingBot-World v2, HappyOyster-Wandering,
and Genie 3.
The comparison illustrates how each model responds to navigation commands
while maintaining a third-person view of the character and the surrounding
room. The middle frame of LingBot-World v2 shows a duplicated character,
illustrating a scene-consistency failure during navigation.
Visible keyboard indicators denote active controls in the source
recordings.</figcaption>
</figure>

<section id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bench-3: Interleaved text and camera control.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hy-Nomas natively supports interleaved text and camera control within one unified model, without requiring session resets or switching between specialized models. We compare against LingBot-World v2 using its open-source model, evaluating its performance under free-form text instructions. As shown in Figure <a href="#S7.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ Bench-3: Interleaved text and camera control. ‣ 7.3 Comparison with Other World Models ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>,  Hy-Nomas achieves win rate of 75.0% and 73.3% in prompt following and physical plausibility, respectively. For camera control, the two models exhibit more comparable performance, with  Hy-Nomas achieving a win rate of 26.7%. Overall, these results highlight the effectiveness of  Hy-Nomas in maintaining instruction-following accuracy and physical plausibility under interleaved text and camera control.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 17: </span>
<span id="S7.F17.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pairwise human evaluation of spatial memory.</span>
We compare  Hy-Nomas with Genie 3, HappyOyster, and
LingBot-World v2 on 60 shared scenarios involving reversible or
revisiting camera trajectories. We measure how well the model remembers the anchor object and its surrounding environments.

</section>
<section id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bench-4: Spatial memory.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For spatial memory evaluation, we assess whether models can maintain consistent object and scene appearance when revisiting previously observed locations. Human annotators compare the revisited views with their original appearances, focusing on the preservation of scene layout, object identities (<em id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>.<span id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text"></span>, the anchor object), and spatial relationships. A model is considered more spatially consistent if it accurately reconstructs previously observed regions without introducing inconsistent objects, altering scene geometry, or violating spatial relationships.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S7.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ Bench-3: Interleaved text and camera control. ‣ 7.3 Comparison with Other World Models ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> presents the results of the spatial memory evaluation. Compared with Genie 3,  Hy-Nomas achieves a win rate of 13.3%, a tie rate of 56.7%, and a loss rate of 30.0%, indicating that Genie 3 maintains stronger spatial consistency. Genie supports grounding in Street View data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rivas et al., 2026</a>)</cite>; we hypothesize that may contribute to improved spatial consistency. Against HappyOyster,  Hy-Nomas achieves comparable performance, with 30.0% wins, 46.7% ties, and 23.3% losses. In contrast,  Hy-Nomas substantially outperforms LingBot-World v2, achieving a win rate of 58.3% and a loss rate of only 1.7%. Overall, these results demonstrate the competitive spatial memory capabilities of  Hy-Nomas, while highlighting a remaining gap with Genie 3. We hypothesize that incorporating more data with looped camera trajectories during training could further improve spatial memory consistency. We leave this for future research explorations. Figure <a href="#S7.F18" title="Figure 18 ‣ Bench-4: Spatial memory. ‣ 7.3 Comparison with Other World Models ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> illustrates a spatial memory example in a scene with a red toolbox on a wooden workbench. Comparing the initial view of the anchor object and surrounding environment, later views make changes to object appearance and scene structure.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.F18" class="ltx_figure">
<div id="S7.F18.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:129.7pt;vertical-align:-0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-82.6pt,31.0pt) scale(0.676323054552542,0.676323054552542) ;"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S7.F18.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="265.37" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 701.23 265.37" width="701.23"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="translate(0,265.37) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(0,265.38)"><g stroke-width="0.4pt"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 0 -33.9)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:4.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:1.39em;font-size:10pt;" height="28.9" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="62.27"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S7.F18.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_top" style="width:4.5em;">
<span id="S7.F18.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"></span>
<span id="S7.F18.pic1.1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S7.F18.pic1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_sansserif" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Input

<div id="S7.F18.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:400.5pt;height:55.5pt;vertical-align:-0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" <figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 18: </span><span id="S7.F18.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qualitative comparison of spatial memory under viewpoint revisitation.</span>

 Hy-Nomas and Genie 3 retain the closed toolbox in

</section>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.4 </span>LoRA Adaption Results</h3>

<div id="S7.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We merge the LoRA weights trained on the base autoregressive model into the distilled model, which we recommend as the best practice for LoRA adaptation. We refer to the resulting model as the LoRA-adapted model.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cinematic LoRA Results.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Compared with the distilled model, the cinematic LoRA-adapted model produces a more visually appealing cinematic style, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S7.F19" title="Figure 19 ‣ Robotics LoRA Results. ‣ 7.4 LoRA Adaption Results ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>.
We further evaluate both models on Bench-1 for multi-turn text interaction, assessing prompt following and physical plausibility, and on Bench-2 for camera control, to examine whether the improvements in cinematic visual quality introduce any regressions in other capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Quantitative results are reported in Figure <a href="#S7.F20" title="Figure 20 ‣ Robotics LoRA Results. ‣ 7.4 LoRA Adaption Results ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a>. Human evaluation demonstrates a strong preference for the adapted model in terms of fewer visual artifacts and improved text-prompt following. On Bench-1, the LoRA-SFT model shows improvements in both prompt following and physical plausibility, achieving win rates of <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="35\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>35</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">35\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="46\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>46</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">46\%</annotation></semantics></math>, compared to loss rates of <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="24\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>24</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">24\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="13\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">13\%</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. However, we observe a moderate regression in camera-control performance, with the LoRA-SFT model achieving a <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="19\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>19</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">19\%</annotation></semantics></math> win rate versus a <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="37\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>37</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">37\%</annotation></semantics></math> loss rate. We hypothesize that this degradation stems from the limited diversity of camera trajectories in the SFT dataset, which may weaken previously learned camera-control capabilities, particularly for underrepresented camera motions. These results highlight the effectiveness of LoRA in adapting visual styles with minimal training data, while underscoring the importance of preserving diverse control signals during fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Robotics LoRA Results.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to the distilled model as a baseline, illustrated in Figure <a href="#S7.F19" title="Figure 19 ‣ Robotics LoRA Results. ‣ 7.4 LoRA Adaption Results ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>, the merged robotics-specific distilled checkpoint can perform out-of-distribution dual-arm tasks, while the baseline confuses the generation of dual-arm and human hands due to the heavy training set distribution of human egocentric data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.F19" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.36729v1/LoRA_SFT_Comparison.png" id="S7.F19.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/312;" width="429" height="312" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 19: </span><span id="S7.F19.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qualitative results of LoRA-SFT.</span> We compare the distilled model with domain-specific LoRA-SFT variants. The upper examples show improved cinematic aesthetics after cinematic LoRA-SFT, while the lower examples show more physically plausible robotic manipulation, with cup deformation more faithfully reflecting the gripper’s applied pressure. <span id="S7.F19.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LoRA-SFT</span> denotes the distilled model with the trained LoRA weights merged into it.</figcaption>
</figure>

and camera control on Bench-2.

and losses (pink) from the perspective of LoRA-SFT

<span id="S7.F21.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rank-gap-weighted human evaluation of Hy-Nomas-PE (ours).</span>

</figure>
<div id="S7.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also evaluate the performance of our PE model by end-to-end directly comparison. We consider three different models: Hy-Nomas-PE, the original Qwen3.8-27B, and Kimi-K3. Figure <a href="#S7.F21" title="Figure 21 ‣ 7.5 PE Results ‣ 7 Evaluation ‣ Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a> presents the evaluation results on Bench-1 and Bench-3. Compared to Qwen3.8-27B, our PE achieves substantial improvements in both prompt following and physical plausibility while maintaining the camera control performance, significantly narrowing the performance gap with Kimi-K3. Besides, our PE achieves a nearly 100% success rate in adhering to the required response format for user inputs, compared to approximately 50% for Qwen3.8-27B and 70% for Kimi-K3.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">World models</h5>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The definition of world model now encompasses a broad range of objectives and approaches. Representation-based approaches, such as V-JEPA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bardes et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, learn predictive visual features as a foundation for video understanding. Geometry-based approaches, including systems from World Labs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">World Labs, 2025</a>)</cite>, emphasize persistent 3D representations that support rendering and navigation. Reconstruction models such as VGGT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> provide complementary building blocks for recovering scene geometry from visual observations. Video-based approaches model world evolution through generated observations, drawing on large collections of videos to learn visual dynamics and action-conditioned transitions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bruce et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. A central question is whether learning from visual appearances and motion alone is sufficient to capture the underlying physical dynamics, or whether additional structural priors and supervision are required. Controlled studies have revealed limitations in the physical generalization of video generation models, even as model capacity and training data scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Meanwhile, recent work has demonstrated that post-training techniques, such as DPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wallace et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rafailov et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, can improve physical consistency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cai et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Nevertheless, whether further scaling of data and model capacity, combined with reinforcement learning (RL), can fundamentally overcome these limitations and enable video-generation-based world models to learn robust physical dynamics remains an open research question. 
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this sense, world modeling brings together several long-standing goals of computer vision: 3D reconstruction, video understanding, and visual generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib125" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib133" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib135" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bahmani et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. It also raises a broader question: can intelligence emerge from perceiving the visual world? A complementary direction uses a language- or vision-language-model agent to write and refine Blender code for constructing or editing 3D scenes, as explored in BlenderAlchemy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Such a pipeline could additionally incorporate generative video editing to enhance visual realism. This design places planning and program synthesis in an agent, while delegating scene execution and rendering to graphics tools. It illustrates a possible division of responsibilities, without establishing where intelligence must reside. Whether multimodal learning contributes distinct forms of intelligence beyond providing interfaces for perception and generation remains an open question. 
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Across these approaches, world models offer promising applications in autonomous driving <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib126" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib127" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib132" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib128" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, robotics and action-conditioned simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib129" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib130" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib131" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib136" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and controllable game generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bruce et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib113" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib111" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib123" title="" class="ltx_ref">Valevski et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib124" title="" class="ltx_ref">Che et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib105" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.  Hy-Nomas pursues the video-based direction, motivated by the scalability and diversity of available video data. Our focus is on turning this visual experience into interactive generation, where user actions shape subsequent observations and the evolving state of the world.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Video diffusion models</h5>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion models have become a major approach to video generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blattmann et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kodaira et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">HaCohen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team Wan et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blattmann et al., 2023a</a>)</cite> that extend image diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rombach et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saharia et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramesh et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dai et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Betker et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Podell et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black Forest Labs et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Esser et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to temporally coherent video synthesis through spatiotemporal modeling and joint image–video training. Diffusion Transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2023</a>)</cite> establish a scalable backbone for latent diffusion, while Sora <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brooks et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and MovieGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Polyak et al., 2024</a>)</cite> illustrate the potential of large-scale video generation using spacetime latent patches. Seedance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team Seedance and others, 2026</a>)</cite> further advances visual quality and the commercial potential of video generation. In comparison, HunyuanVideo 1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, the backbone of our model, provides an efficient 8B-parameter foundation that balances visual quality with computational accessibility. Beyond fixed-length generation, Diffusion Forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> combines causal sequence prediction with independently sampled noise levels, supporting flexible generation horizons. Self Forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> addresses the training–inference mismatch in autoregressive video diffusion by training on model-generated histories with KV caching. Building on these directions,  Hy-Nomas adapts a pretrained video generator to interactive, segment-wise generation. Its temporally aligned captions, and segment-wise and action-aware attention connect user instructions to specific portions of the rollout, while causal KV caching retains context across successive interactions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Video-based world models</h5>

<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Video-based world models extend video generation toward action-conditioned, interactive environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib112" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Research in this area emphasizes several complementary dimensions, including physical plausibility for physical AI, responsive controllability, and persistent world state. Beyond generating visually convincing sequences, an interactive world model must respond to actions introduced during a rollout and preserve their consequences in subsequent observations. 
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Genie <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bruce et al., 2024</a>)</cite> learns controllable environments from videos without ground-truth action annotations through a latent action model and autoregressive dynamics. Genie 2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google DeepMind, 2024</a>)</cite> and Genie 3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google DeepMind, 2025</a>)</cite> further develop action-controllable environments, with Genie 3 emphasizing real-time interaction and improved visual consistency. LingBot-World v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026b</a>)</cite> explores long-horizon causal generation, more diverse action-control events, and agentic control through pilot
and director components. HappyOyster <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Happy Oyster Team, 2026</a>)</cite> provides interactive world creation through Directing and Wandering modes, which we evaluate for text interaction and camera navigation, respectively. 
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These approaches share challenges in responsive control, physical plausibility, spatial memory, and efficient long-horizon generation. Within this direction,  Hy-Nomas focuses on native alternation between free-form textual instructions and continuous camera control in one 8B model. It combines temporally structured supervision, persistent causal context, and a VLM-based director that translates user intent into segment-level prompts and generation durations. Our evaluation examines text interaction, camera control, interleaved control, and spatial memory separately to characterize these complementary capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">9 </span>Discussion and Future Directions</h2>

<section id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Gaming and robotics.</h5>

<div id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Gaming and robotics place different demands on world models. For gaming, a practical challenge is how quickly the model responds to a player’s input. Turning the camera or issuing an action should produce a visual response with minimal delay, while repeated interactions should preserve scene consistency. Distillation can reduce the number of denoising steps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib114" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib122" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and quantization can reduce memory use and computational cost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib118" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. These gains must be evaluated alongside visual quality and consistency over long rollouts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib115" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2026b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib109" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>. For robotics, the challenge extends beyond generating a plausible response: the predicted outcome must match the effect of an executable robot action <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib116" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib117" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026c</a>)</cite>. For example, a grasp prediction should reflect whether the gripper makes contact with an object and successfully lifts it. World-action models such as DreamZero <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2026</a>)</cite> jointly predict actions and future visual states, providing a potential route toward this capability. Adapting  Hy-Nomas to robotic control would require training on videos paired with robot actions and evaluating whether its predictions support successful task execution. Datasets such as Open X-Embodiment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib119" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khazatsky et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024</a>)</cite> provide a starting point, although coverage across tasks, environments, and robot embodiments remains limited. As an initial step in this direction, we demonstrate LoRA-based fine tuning on robotics adaptation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agentic world models.</h5>

<div id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Long-horizon world generation requires remembering previously observed scenes to maintain consistency when users revisit them. Retaining the full KV cache on the GPU becomes increasingly costly as rollouts grow. One possible approach is to offload older context to CPU memory or persistent storage and selectively retrieve information relevant to the next segment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib120" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. When a user returns to a room, for example, the system could retrieve earlier views of that room rather than attend to the entire interaction history. WorldMem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2025</a>)</cite> demonstrates the value of retrieving historical observations for consistency when revisiting scenes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Different types of information may benefit from different memory representations: geometry can encode spatial relationships, reference images can preserve visual appearance, and text can summarize events and state changes, such as a door being opened or an object being moved <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib121" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. (2025b)</a></cite>. In our spatial-memory experiments, explicitly describing the expected scene content when revisiting a location can improve consistency. An agent could use this mechanism to specify which objects should reappear, where they should be, and what has changed since the previous visit, while visual references could help preserve their precise appearance. Cached keys and values offer another form of memory by retaining features that the generator can directly reuse, although managing their GPU memory footprint requires offloading, compression, or eviction. A practical agentic system would coordinate these memory representations, retrieve relevant information, and update stored records as the world evolves, ensuring that outdated observations do not override the current scene state. 
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Retrieval alone, however, cannot account for changes that occur outside the field of view. Consider a wall clock: after the user leaves a room and returns ten minutes later, the clock should remain in the same place with the same appearance, but display a time ten minutes later. Reusing an earlier image would recover its appearance without updating its time. An agent could instead record the clock’s identity, location, and observed time, compute its updated state from elapsed simulation time, and pass that state together with a reference image to the generator. Inspired by memory management in language-model agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Packer et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, this approach would expose memory retrieval, state updates, prompt rewriting, and video generation as tools. LingBot-World v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2026b</a>)</cite> provides an encouraging example of agent coordination for interactive world generation. An important next step is to test whether such coordination can maintain explicit world states and render them faithfully over long interactions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data and captioning.</h5>

<div id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite having only 8B parameters,  Hy-Nomas achieves stronger text-driven action control than the larger models evaluated in our benchmark. We hypothesize that accurate, detailed captions contribute to this result by explicitly describing changes over time, which reduces the burden on the diffusion transformer to "imagine" unspecified content and allows it to devote more capacity to just rendering the described scenes and actions correctly. This hypothesis is consistent with findings that improved captions strengthen prompt following in image generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Betker et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. These observations suggest a potential direction for future systems: using highly detailed prompts to specify scene content and temporal evolution, with diffusion models serving primarily as renderers of these descriptions. Such an approach places greater demands on the quality and specificity of both training captions and inference-time prompts, making caption and Prompt Enhancer central challenges. Data curation should therefore consider not only visual quality but also whether the caption accurately describes the video. For example, a clip containing motion blur during a rapid camera turn may still provide useful supervision if the caption describes both the camera motion and the resulting blur. Similarly, explicitly captioning a cut or an editing effect may reduce ambiguity about the observed transition.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Infrastructure and scaling.</h5>

<div id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Higher resolution and longer temporal context increase the number of video tokens, raising training costs, inference latency, and KV-cache memory requirements. Efficient attention, sequence parallelism, and cache management are therefore critical to extending rollouts and enabling interactive generation. These infrastructure advances also make it more practical to explore larger world models. Recent progress in video generation, exemplified by Seedance 2.0 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team Seedance and others, 2026</a>)</cite>, motivates further investigation into the relationship between model capacity and generation quality. MAGI-2 Preview <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sand.ai, 2026</a>)</cite> explores this direction through a mixture-of-experts architecture (MoE), scaling total capacity while limiting the number of parameters activated per token. A central question is whether such investments translate into better world-model capabilities, including actions following, predicting physically consistent outcomes, and preserving scene details when revisiting locations after long rollouts. These capabilities require direct evaluation and cannot be inferred from improvements in visual quality alone.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
